about: Trainer: tangent tracer (Unit 2, the flagship, free). Explore: twelve shelf functions and typed ones (ApCalcExpr), P dragged along f, Q at distance h, the secant and its slope, h toward 0 from both sides with the table of difference quotients, the tangent line on tap, f′ drawn as P moves or traced, one-sided slopes at corners, cusps, vertical tangents, jumps and endpoints (tangentTracer.classify). Test yourself: six seeded kinds from tangentTracer.generate; each context unlocks with its topic. The validator regenerates 300 problems per context and recomputes every key independently.
intro: The derivative is the slope of a curve at one point. You cannot get a slope from one point, so take two: P on the curve and Q a distance $h$ away. The line through them, the secant, has slope $\frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$. In Explore, slide $h$ toward $0$ from either side and watch the secant turn into the tangent line while its slope closes in on $f'(a)$. Move P and the graph of $f'$ draws itself underneath. In Test yourself, estimate derivatives from graphs and tables, pick and sketch the graph of $f'$, write tangent lines and find where $f$ is not differentiable.
howItWorks:
• Secant slope. Through $P = (a, f(a))$ and $Q = (a + h, f(a + h))$ the slope is $\frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$, the average rate of change of $f$ from $a$ to $a + h$. With $h < 0$, Q is to the left of P.
  • The derivative. $f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$, when this limit exists. It is the slope of the tangent line, and the instantaneous rate of change of $f$ at $a$.
  • Tangent line. $y = f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$.
  • Not differentiable. The limit fails at a corner (the one-sided slopes disagree), a cusp (they go to $-\infty$ and $+\infty$), a vertical tangent (both go to $\infty$) and wherever $f$ is not continuous. Differentiable implies continuous; continuous does not imply differentiable.
  • The graph of $f'$. Its height at each $x$ is the slope of $f$ there: positive where $f$ rises, negative where it falls, $0$ at a peak or valley.

The h slider is on a log scale: each step toward the middle makes $h$ about ten times smaller, down to $\pm 0.001$. The tool computes the slopes for the functions on its shelf from their exact derivatives and checks each side of P separately; for a typed function it uses difference quotients with very small $h$. Sketches are graded point by point: the sign, a zero where $f$ has a peak or valley, and the size within about a quarter.
